messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Military Topics: Talks about military, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When the bombing started, Samir had been a relief worker for nearly two decades. He was sixty-four now, a divorced man living alone in a quiet suburb, but the man he had been then—the one who coordinated supply chains through active war zones, who pulled children from rubble while the air burned—felt like a stranger. That stranger had been in a field hospital on the outskirts of a city whose name he no longer said aloud. A shell had landed two hundred meters away. The blast had thrown him against a wall, and for a long moment there was only a high ringing and the smell of burnt wiring, flesh, and diesel. He had crawled through smoke that tasted of metal, his hands finding pieces of people that did not fit together. He remembered the terror not as a story he could tell, but as something that happened to his body: the way his heart slammed against his ribs, the way his vision narrowed to a tunnel of gray. Even now, twenty years later, when the memory returned it came not as a coherent narrative but as disconnected fragments—the sound of a child's shoe hitting concrete, the heat on his face, a single image of a severed hand still wearing a wedding ring. Each fragment carried the same raw terror he had felt in that moment, and when it hit him he would have to stop whatever he was doing, overwhelmed by a wave of emotion that left him breathless and shaking.

Samir had learned to keep this hidden. As a politician—a city councilman in a Midwestern district with a growing Middle Eastern population—he had built a career on composure. He spoke at town halls, shook hands at community events, and sat through long budget meetings. But the world had become a landscape of hidden threats. Silence unnerved him most: a pause in conversation, the hush of a hallway between meetings, the quiet of his own apartment at night. He was certain that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. He checked his doors and windows repeatedly before bed, sometimes three or four times, and he scanned every room he entered for exits, for shadows, for anyone who seemed out of place. He could not help it; his eyes moved constantly, reading faces, reading hands, reading the space around him for signs of ambush.

His work had become his shield. He threw himself into tasks—drafting policy proposals, returning calls, attending evening events—because keeping his mind occupied meant less room for the fragments to surface. He tried hard to control his emotions, especially in public. When a constituent brought up military funding at a meeting, he felt his chest tighten and his mouth go dry, but he nodded and changed the subject. When someone shook his hand too firmly, he felt a flash of the old panic and pulled away. He avoided talking to strangers whenever possible, delegating small talk to his aide. And burnt smells—a neighbor's barbecue, a car backfiring, the toaster left on too long—sent him into a cold sweat that he masked with a cough and a quick exit.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. His marriage had ended years ago, in part because his wife could not understand why he would not go to restaurants with open kitchens or why he flinched when she touched him from behind. His relationships with his adult children were strained; they saw him as distant, work-obsessed, unreachable. He had stopped attending mosque because the crowded room and the sudden silences during prayer felt unbearable. His colleagues respected him but found him guarded, hard to read.

What finally brought Samir to seek help was a city council hearing on a new housing development near an old industrial site. A member of the public had stood up and described the demolition process, using the word "blast." Samir had felt the floor drop out from under him. He had excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood with his hands on the sink, shaking, the smell of burnt dust from the construction site drifting through a window. He had looked at his face in the mirror—sixty-four years old, tired, alone—and had understood that he could not keep managing this by himself. He was afraid of what might happen if he let the memories come fully, afraid that he would fall apart and never piece himself back together. But he was also afraid of spending the rest of his life checking locks and flinching at silence. He wanted, more than anything, to sleep through the night without waking to the smell of smoke.
